question.leadin: King Charles III ascended to the throne when this woman died.
question.text: Name this British queen who died in September 2022, prompting widespread mourning across the Commonwealth.
question.answerHtml: Queen Elizabeth II [prompt on Elizabeth; do NOT accept or prompt on "Elizabeth I"]
question.clue: In addition to a 19th-century figure, protestors in Manitoba toppled a statue of this person following the 2021 discovery of a mass grave of Indigenous boarding school children.

swap.leadin: This vessel from the Cunard Line was named after the Roman province that included modern-day Portugal.
swap.text: Name this British ocean liner, the world's largest passenger ship at the time, that was sunk in 1915 off the coast of Ireland.
swap.clue: Travelers on this ship were warned that a "state of war exists" by a newspaper ad plaed by the Imperial German Embassy.

question.leadin: This war ended with the creation of the Protectorate and the execution of King Charles I.
question.text: Name this war, which saw a clash between factions known as the Cavaliers and Roundheads. The Long Parliament essentially ruled its namesake country during this war.
question.clue: This conflict's second phase saw the defeat of Scottish forces at Preston, after which the victorious commander perpetrated the massacre at Drogheda to punish Irish supporters of his enemies.

swap.leadin: This ruler's most significant victory was preceded by a landing at Pevensey.
swap.text: Name this Norman who was crowned on Christmas 1066 after winning the Battle of Hastings over Harold Godwinson.
swap.answerHtml: William I (accept William the Conqueror; accept William the Bastard)
swap.clue: An Archbishop of Canterbury named Stigand stands next to this ruler in one depiction commissioned by his half-brother Odo.

question.leadin: She was also known as Alexandrina.
question.text: Name this monarch whose reign was the longest in British history until Elizabeth II's overtook it in 2015.
question.clue: As a child, this monarch was told never to leave the presence of the Duchess of Kent as one of eight rules imposed while they both lived in Kensington Palace.

swap.leadin: This 1982 conflict was between Argentina and the United Kingdom.
swap.text: Leopoldo Galtieri ordered the Argentine armed forces to invade a South Atlantic archipelago in this war. The Argentine Admiral Jorge Anaya did not expect a response from the British military.
swap.clue: This conflict began when one side's troops landed on April 2, and ended when they were forced to give up the territorial capital of Port Stanley in mid-June of the same year.

question.text: Alfred also sponsored the creation of a Chronicle named for these people. These people, the main medieval inhabitants of modern England, took their hyphenated name from two Germanic tribes that settled there.
question.clue: These people were protected by forts called burhs during the Heptarchy.

swap.leadin: Some troops involved in this battle were stationed near the church of St. Ninian.
swap.text: Name this 1314 battle in which Edward II failed to relieve a siege on Stirling Castle, losing to the troops of Robert the Bruce.
swap.clue: Action in this battle was preceded by an agreement between one commander's brother and Sir Philip Mowbray in which Mowbray's castle garrison would be forced to surrender by June 24.

question.text: At Braemar, Lord Mar proclaimed James Francis Edward Stuart, also known as the Old Pretender, to be king of this country. This country was united with its southern neighbor, England, through the Act of Union.
question.clue: Peter and Eileen Caddy founded the New Age Findhorn Community in this country.

swap.leadin: The battle of this location during World War I saw the sinking of all but one of the ships commanded by Maximilian von Spee, ending threats to Allied possessions in the region.
swap.text: Identify this geographical entity, the subject of a war that saw the sinking of the HMS Sheffield by an Exocet missile.
swap.clue: An undeclared war over this archipelago and the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands was fought when Leopoldo Galtieri claimed sovereignty over Las Islas Malvinas.

question.leadin: Answer these questions about a British politician.
question.text: is considered the first British prime minister, a position he began to hold during this monarch's reign.

swap.leadin: This man allied with Henry "Hotspur" Percy of Northumberland in a rebellion against the English king.
swap.text: Name this Welsh revolutionary who led a namesake 15th century revolt and is the last native Welshman to hold the title "Prince of Wales."
swap.answerHtml: Owain Glyndŵr (“oh-WINE glin-DOOWR”) [or Owain ap Gruffydd; accept, but glare at and correct, Owen Glendower; accept Glyndŵr Rising or Glyndŵr Rebellion]
swap.clue: After a neighbourly dispute with Reginald Grey, an amnesty was issued to this man's followers by Henry "Hotspur" Percy, who was killed at the Battle of Shrewsbury.

question.leadin: This law stated that the requirement to own land was to merely live in a house with a hearth sufficient to boil a pot.
question.text: Identify this 1832 law that massively changed the English and Welsh electoral system, expanded the franchise and eliminated so-called "pocket" and "rotten boroughs".
question.answerHtml: Representation of the People Act 1832 [Accept Great Reform Act 1832 or 1832 Reform Act or First Reform Act]

swap.text: This hoax involved the discovery of a fake skeleton in Sussex that claimed to be a missing link between humans and apes. Actually a combination of human and orangutan bones, this hoax was created by amateur archaeologist Charles Dawson.
swap.answerHtml: Piltdown Man hoax [or Piltdown forgery or Piltdown Man forgery or Piltdown hoax]

question.text: The term "eugenics" was first coined by this British scientist, who advocated arranged marriages in Hereditary Genius. He set up an endowment to create a namesake chair for eugenics that employed Karl Pearson.

swap.text: Before Iraqi independence, Britain passed this 1931 piece of legislation, granting Imperial Dominions legislative independence. This legislation gave effect to many of the resolutions of the Imperial Conferences of 1926 and 1930.
swap.clue: Passed at the end of 1931, this twelve section act formally upheld the autonomy of the dominions of the British Commonwealth, such as Canada and the Irish Free State.

question.text: The Duke of York became a major court power after this revolt of 1450 in which men from Kent and Sussex marched on London.
question.clue: The rebels were victorious at Sevenoaks, but looting in London led to them being driven out.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about quotes often mis-attributed to a politician.
swap.text: In an apocryphal story, Churchill told this woman "If I were married to you, I'd put poison in your coffee," to which she replied "If I were married to you, I'd drink it." She was the first woman to sit in the British parliament, though her Nazi sympathies got her into trouble in the 1940s.
swap.clue: This woman, the first to take her parliamentary seat in the House of Commons. This woman founded the Cliveden Set, a club of Nazi sympathizers that pushed for appeasement.

question.leadin: Identify these people important in the rise of British maritime power.
question.text: This man vigorously promoted Elizabethan overseas exploration and his major work, The Principal Navigations, Voyages, and Discoveries of the English Nation, is the most comprehensive account of early English voyages to North America.
question.clue: This writer of The Principal Navigations, Voyages, and Discoveries of the English Nations first translated Grotius's Mare Liberum into English. He names a London-based society that publishes primary accounts of historic maritime voyages.

swap.text: This man pretended to be Richard of Shrewsbury, the younger son of Edward IV. With support from his ostensible aunt, Margaret of York, he invaded from Scotland in 1496 and again from Cornwall in 1497 before being captured and eventually hanged.
swap.clue: This man married Lady Catherine Gordon whilst a guest of James IV of Scotland, and he led the Second Cornish Uprising after landing at Whitesand Bay in 1497.
